title: BIRD Foundation Backs Qarakal Quantum and Quantum Elements for Quantum-Accelerated Catalysis Modeling - Quantum Computing Report
gist: The Israel-U.S. BIRD Foundation approved a conditional grant for Qarakal Quantum (Tel Aviv) and Quantum Elements (California) to build an MVP that uses quantum algorithms to simulate heterogeneous surface catalysis, where classical DFT and post-Hartree-Fock methods struggle. The project is one of seven picked in BIRD's September 2026 cycle, which awarded $7.4 million to unlock about $20 million in project investment through non-dilutive, royalty-repaid grants capped at $1.5 million.

insights.claim: In its September 2026 cycle, the BIRD Foundation Board of Governors selected seven Israel-US deep-tech collaborations and awarded $7.4 million in conditional grants, expected to unlock about $20 million in total public-private project investment.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Each BIRD dollar draws roughly 2.7 dollars of total project spend, a modest but leveraged source of binational deep-tech funding.
insights.locator: The partnership is one of seven deep-tech collaborations

insights.claim: BIRD grants are evaluated by reviewers appointed by NIST and the Israel Innovation Authority. They fund up to 50% of a project budget, capped at $1.5 million, on a non-dilutive basis and are repaid through royalties once commercial revenue starts.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Non-dilutive, royalty-repaid funding lets early quantum software startups extend runway without equity dilution.
insights.locator: Evaluated by reviewers appointed by the National Institute

insights.claim: Since 1977, BIRD has invested about $470 million across more than 1,200 bilateral projects. It is taking executive summaries for its next cycle through November 23, 2026, with decisions due in March 2027.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: The next funding decisions in March 2027 are a datapoint for Israel-US quantum startup activity.
insights.locator: The grant represents the latest quantum chemistry award

insights.claim: Qarakal Quantum (Tel Aviv) and Quantum Elements (Westlake Village, CA) will use BIRD funding to build a minimum viable product that integrates quantum algorithms to simulate heterogeneous surface catalysis. It will compute active-site binding energies and kinetic pathways so chemical manufacturers can discover and refine industrial catalysts.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Industrial chemistry is one of the earliest candidate markets for quantum advantage, and this is an MVP-stage entry to watch for customer pilots.

insights.claim: Classical supercomputers struggle with catalytic surface reactions because electron-correlation effects at active catalyst sites require multi-reference methods that scale factorially. DFT and post-Hartree-Fock approximations therefore often hit precision limits when predicting reaction barriers and intermediate states.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: This is the technical rationale for quantum chemistry's value proposition. Gains depend on quantum hardware reaching the scale needed for strongly correlated systems.
insights.locator: Addressing Electronic Structure Bottlenecks in Catalytic Reactions

insights.claim: Target applications for the Qarakal-Quantum Elements platform include predictive catalyst design for chemical manufacturing, green hydrogen generation and battery interfaces.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: This links quantum chemistry to energy-transition themes such as hydrogen and batteries, where better catalyst and interface models could reduce costs.
